overview: Ass4Sale revolves around the phenomenon of twerking, a dance form that has gained increasing popularity in western culture since Miley Cyrus’ uncritical appropriation in 2013. Rezaire investigates the mechanisms of cultural appropriation that have stripped twerking of its African origins and culture. As a former ritual of fertility, twerking is strongly tied to the black female body. Assimilated and disseminated as a mainstream phenomena and commodity fetish, it has been decontextualised from issues of race, gender, privilege and ownership. title: Hometown Mutonia
overview: A documentary film about the Mutoids’ camp in Santarcangelo di Romagna, a medieval little village in the middle of Italy, near Rimini.  Mutonia is a strange village inside a village, a temporary town which has been transformed over time, relating to a bigger urban, territorial and social context. It was born out of the anarchic, iconoclastic and experimental spirit of the travellers and cyber punks who founded it; the town has been home to two generations of travellers and has become a place of origin, a “motherland” to come back to, or to stop and raise children.  This original living place, made up of assembled scrap and vehicles transformed at home, now risks extinction, because there is no urban regulation which accounts for such an anomaly, which at its core was created by everyday life and invention, fragility and energy, transgression and the need for roots.

If, as Sergio Quinzio suggests, prayer is a negative moment marked by God’s constant lack of response, the first part, freely inspired by Silvio D’Arzo’s  Casa d’altri, explores this question through a single figure. A wanderer moves among saints, churches and books, posing a scandalous question to theology. The second part shifts the same question from the individual to the multitude. Through archival materials connected to rites, processions and popular pilgrimages, the film observes bodies that pray, walk, wait, and offer fatigue, voice, tears and presence. Following Quinzio’s intuition, the praying figures do not appear as pacified images of devotion, but as needy creatures, beggars before the invisible, bodies asking for the fulfilment of a concrete lack.

As a clue, he sent me a photocopied manuscript of ​the novel “The Fourbanks of the River of Space” by ​the South American novelist Wilson Harris, who lived nearby. Afterthoughts of a Walk on the Naze is ​a​ quantum fiction that attempts to ​answer his letter. overview: Minimal interventions to a single roll of film can have surprising effects. Overhead cables seen from a moving train are filmed on a three-minute camera roll. The second half of the film uses a spare print, sliced down the middle and taped back together with a slight mis-alignment that leaves a vertical fissure running down through the film. This is also printed three times, and also projected with one of the films flipped. The varying running speeds of the projectors create a natural and unpredictable phasing between the three images. (Guy Sherwin)

title: Remjet
overview: Looking through my outdated film stock for a hand-made project to use in my teaching, I started experimenting with raw colour film. Colour stock is tricky to use because of its Remjet backing which blocks the light from bouncing around during exposure (it is removed in the processing). However, if you scratch lines into both sides of the film, the points at which they cross create points of light, and this registers as sound if it appears in the optical soundtrack area. This is the simple technique that formed the basis of Remjet. The work then was to build up patterns of lines and tones and to organise them into a viable projection performance. The resulting interference patterns suggested the variable frequencies of FM radio as a random element to add to the performance. (Guy Sherwin)

title: And the Trees Danced Below
overview: Uzbek youth confess their dreams, take flight, and negotiate the reality around them. Directed by Kirill Kulagin.  In this documentary directed by Kirill Kulagin, Uzbek teenagers share their innermost dreams. And rather than talk of only fantasies, these dreams unearth the reality these youth face and how they negotiate with it.  In Central Asia, talking about oneself can seem impolite. From an outsider perspective, emotions in this culture are only spoken about indirectly, lest they “air [their] dirty laundry in public.” But talking about dreams can break through this social barrier.  For the film, Kulagin ran filmmaking labs with Uzbek youth to explore their real stories and real feelings surrounding dreams. These dreams served as jumping-off points to discuss deeper fears and desires, which turned into metaphors and a visual language based on how they navigated the boundaries of intimacy.

title: The door was left ajar...
overview: This short experimental film explores the trace of a fragmented female voice. She speaks—but never appears. Her voice feels like a private call, drifting through absence, never fully arriving. The visuals do not explain or support the voice—they drift beside it:  fragments of eroded imagery, textures that resemble old celluloid, moments that feel lost even as they appear.  Surreal motifs—shadows, archival blur, abstract surfaces—form a visual grammar of dislocation. The woman is not in the frame. She interrupts it. She haunts it. She is memory without image, presence without body.  This is not a story. It is a residue—an audiovisual monologue on loss, distortion, and what remains when time corrodes experience. What we see and what we hear never fully meet.  The result is a cinematic space of rupture, where memory is not recalled but  re-performed—through ghostly impressions, through the illusion of continuity. The film is about what refuses to be resolved.

The arrival of a new employee, Sergei, leads her into adultery and then crime, making her more akin to Lady Macbeth. But unlike Shakespeare’s character, Katerina acts not out of a thirst for power but to satisfy urges stifled by a sordid environment.  Premiered in 1934 in Leningrad when Dmitri Shostakovich was only 28 years old, Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk was a triumph that nevertheless sealed the composer’s fate. Stalin deemed the opera scandalous and incompatible with “socialist realism”. The composer was threatened with deportation and the work banned for more than 25 years before resurfacing in a diluted version.  Performed in its original version, Shostakovich’s powerful and tense score is reinforced by Krzysztof Warlikowski’s staging. By placing the characters in a slaughterhouse, he restores this 20th century masterpiece’s unflinching brutality.

title: Film d'entraînement
overview: A seemingly innocuous sequence drawn from a DVD calibration menu becomes the starting point for a film that slips away from its own premise. An Asian woman wanders through a sunlit lagoon landscape accompanied by a syrupy soundtrack, until a synthetic voice interrupts the image: “This image is to test the sound and the color.” From this point onward, the film unfolds in three movements that gradually dissolve the boundary between function and narrative. What begins as a parody of self-help or training videos shifts into an intimate documentary on the preparation of a film, before being abruptly disrupted by the intrusion of the material conditions of filmmaking itself, where completion appears as both necessity and impossibility. The work situates itself in the space of rehearsal and process, where a filmmaker, at home or in transit, is indistinguishable from the act of making, and where the film exists only as it is being assembled.

title: Minuit passé

An attempt to make a film together becomes less a project than a deferred encounter, complicated by familiarity and the refusal of fiction as mask. Gradually, attention shifts from staging and narration to the fragile act of transmission itself: the way dreams must be reshaped into stories in order to be shared, even as they resist such translation. In this interval between lived experience and its articulation, the possibility of a different cinema emerges, one attentive to what happens before and after the image, in the neglected folds where life precedes form and exceeds it.

However, their design could give rise to an infinite number of variations and whimsical interpretations... In this video, “FIN” becomes the main character. Playful, it changes its “costume” each time, literally bursting through the screen, relentlessly and inexorably crushing the fragments of action visible beneath it. overview: In this acclaimed lecture, historian Robin Lane Fox examines Alexander the Great's relationship with the divine and the origins of ruler worship in the Hellenistic world. Drawing on ancient texts, archaeology, and newly studied Egyptian inscriptions, he argues that Alexander sincerely believed he enjoyed a special relationship with Zeus-Ammon, while stopping short of considering himself a fully immortal god.  Lane Fox challenges the view that Alexander imposed his divinity on others, showing instead how Greek cities and followers voluntarily granted him extraordinary honours in recognition of his unprecedented achievements. He then explores how Alexander's successors—Ptolemy, Seleucus, Antigonus, and others—expanded this tradition, transforming the political and religious landscape of the ancient Mediterranean.  A fascinating reappraisal of kingship, religion, and Alexander's enduring legacy.
